cues.text: A Boy Consecrated Early

Born Francesco Forgione in 1887 in Pietrelcina, a small town in southern Italy, the future saint reported experiencing visions and spiritual phenomena from early childhood and consecrated himself to Jesus at only five years old.
Entering the Capuchin Franciscans at fifteen, he took the name Pio and, despite chronic poor health that repeatedly interrupted his studies, was ordained a priest in 1910.
Wartime Service and Illness
Padre Pio was drafted into the Italian army during the First World War but was discharged after being diagnosed with tuberculosis.
In 1916 he was assigned to the remote friary of Our Lady of Grace at San Giovanni Rotondo , in the Gargano mountains of southern Italy.
He would remain there for the rest of his life — more than fifty years — apart from brief absences.
The Stigmata
On 20 September 1918, while making his thanksgiving after Mass, Padre Pio reported a vision of Christ.
When the vision ended, he discovered visible wounds in his hands, feet, and side corresponding to the wounds of the crucifixion—the stigmata .
They remained open and visible on his body for the rest of his life, examined repeatedly by physicians without a natural medical explanation ever being established to the Church's satisfaction.
Years of Suspicion
The stigmata, along with widespread reports of other extraordinary phenomena attributed to him, drew intense curiosity.
These included bilocation and an unusual gift for perceiving the sins of those who came to him for confession, as well as suspicion from both medical authorities and the Church itself.

In 1924 and again in 1931, Vatican authorities restricted him from publicly celebrating Mass or hearing confessions while his case was investigated; Padre Pio accepted these restrictions, later reversed, without public complaint.
An Extraordinary Confessor
Once restored to full ministry, Padre Pio became known above all as a confessor of remarkable spiritual insight.
He spent as many as ten to fifteen hours a day in the confessional, drawing pilgrims from across Italy and eventually the world.
Many of these pilgrims reported that he seemed to know their sins before they had spoken them.

In 1956 he also founded a modern hospital, the Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza ('House for the Relief of Suffering'), at San Giovanni Rotondo, which remains a major regional medical center to this day.
Legacy
Padre Pio died at San Giovanni Rotondo in 1968, and was canonized in 2002 by Pope John Paul II .
The shrine built around his tomb draws roughly eight million pilgrims annually, second in Catholic pilgrimage numbers only to the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe.
This testifies to the enduring devotion inspired by a friar who bore, visibly and for half a century, the wounds of the Passion.
He spent his life helping others approach them through the confessional.
